opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that protein language models have been trained on millions of protein sequences, essentially the record of what evolution has tried over billions of years. To predict masked amino acids or the next residue well, these models have to internalize a lot of biology: which residues co-vary, which structural motifs recur, what makes a binding site or a transmembrane region. Nobody told the model about any of that. It discovered those regularities on its own from raw sequence.

So when we open up the model, say with sparse autoencoders to pull apart the internal representations into more interpretable features, we're not just debugging a piece of software. We're asking what the model has learned about proteins, and some of what it has learned may be things we, as biologists, don't fully understand yet.

That's what makes it feel like discovery rather than engineering. In a lot of interpretability work on text models, we already know the concepts we're looking for: grammar, sentiment, factual knowledge. We can check whether a feature corresponds to something we recognize. With proteins, many of the features we find do map cleanly onto known annotations, like secondary structure, specific domains, catalytic residues, or post-translational modification sites, and that's a good sanity check. But some features are coherent and consistent across many proteins without matching any existing database annotation. Those are the exciting ones. They could be gaps in our annotations, or patterns that point to biological functions or mechanisms that haven't been characterized.

So the workflow starts to look like the scientific method. The model gives you a hypothesis: here's a feature that fires on this particular set of residues across these protein families. Then you go and figure out what it means. You look at structures, check the literature, maybe design experiments. In a sense the model becomes a microscope for looking at evolutionary data, and interpretability is how we learn to read what that microscope shows.

I think this is a broader shift. As AI models get trained on more scientific data, like genomics, single-cell data, and materials, they'll pick up structure in that data that's hard for humans to see directly. Interpretability becomes a way to turn the model's implicit knowledge into explicit scientific insight we can test, build on, and trust.

r001.rationale: The response says protein models learn coherent features that lack existing annotations and may reveal biological functions or mechanisms that have not yet been characterized.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that a protein language model like ESM has been trained on hundreds of millions of sequences, and in the process it's learned something about proteins that we didn't explicitly teach it. It predicts structure, it predicts the effects of mutations, it does things that took biologists decades of experiments to figure out. So the question that keeps nagging at me is: what does it actually know? And more importantly, does it know anything we don't?

That reframes interpretability. Normally when people talk about interpreting a model, the goal is something like safety or debugging, understanding why the model made a particular prediction so we can trust it or fix it. That's valuable, but with protein models I think there's a second, more exciting goal. These models are essentially a compressed summary of evolution. Every sequence they saw is the result of billions of years of selection, and the model has had to find regularities across all of that to predict the next amino acid. If it found a regularity that corresponds to a known biological concept, great, that's validation. But if it found one that doesn't map onto anything in the textbooks, that's a hypothesis. That's a candidate for new biology.

So in our work, when we pull apart the internal features of these models, we're doing something that looks a lot like what a biologist does when they look at data. We find a feature, we ask what sequences activate it, we look at where in the structure those residues sit, we check whether it lines up with annotations like binding sites or structural motifs. Many of the features do line up with things we know, which is reassuring. But a meaningful fraction don't have a clean existing label, and those are the ones I find most interesting. We've had cases where a feature fires on a set of residues that looked unrelated at first, and only after digging did we realize it was tracking something like a particular contact pattern or a functional constraint that wasn't well characterized.

There's also a practical side. Biologists have an enormous number of experiments they could run and limited time and money. If the model has already noticed that a certain region behaves in a certain way across a huge diversity of proteins, that's a free, cheap signal about where to look. So interpretability becomes a hypothesis-generating tool. The model does the pattern finding over data at a scale no human could read, and the human does the part of deciding whether the pattern is real and what it means.

The honest caveat is that the model can also learn artifacts. It can pick up on database biases, on which organisms got sequenced the most, on quirks of how sequences were curated. Part of treating this as science rather than just engineering is being disciplined about that, treating each feature as a claim that needs independent evidence, not as a fact because the model found it. But I'd say that's exactly what makes it feel like discovery to me. You have a strange, very capable instrument that has observed more of protein space than any person ever will, and you're trying to work out what it's seeing.

r001.rationale: The response explains that interpreting model features can reveal patterns with no existing biological label, making them hypotheses or candidates for new biology that humans have not yet identified.

astra-6.text:
Because with protein language models, we’re trying to discover something about biology, not just understand how a piece of software works. These models learn from protein sequences, and those sequences reflect the outcomes of evolution. To model them well, the model can pick up patterns related to protein structure and function, even without being explicitly taught those concepts.

So the interesting question is: What has it learned? If we can identify an internal feature that corresponds to a biological property, that gives us a way to connect the model’s representations to scientific concepts. And potentially, there are features that capture something we haven’t characterized yet.

That’s where interpretation becomes a discovery process. We can use it to generate a hypothesis—for example, that a particular sequence pattern affects a protein’s function—and then test that experimentally. The model itself doesn’t establish that the hypothesis is true. But it can help us find promising questions that we might not have thought to ask.

r001.rationale: The response says interpretation can reveal model features capturing biological properties that have not yet been characterized, framing this as a way to generate new scientific hypotheses.

sol-6.1.text:
I think what makes this exciting is that proteins are a language that we don’t fully understand. We can measure their sequences, and we know that those sequences determine a tremendous amount about their structure and function, but the rules connecting those things are still only partially understood.

When we train a protein language model on many sequences, it learns statistical patterns that reflect some of those biological constraints. So interpreting the model becomes a way to ask: What has it picked up about biology? Does a particular feature correspond to a structural motif, an interaction, or some aspect of protein function?

The scientific discovery part comes when we go beyond finding something we already recognize. If the model has learned a pattern that doesn’t correspond to an existing annotation, that can give us a hypothesis. We can then design experiments to test whether that pattern actually matters. The interpretation itself isn’t proof, but it can help us identify questions we wouldn’t otherwise have thought to ask.

r001.rationale: The response says interpretation can reveal a learned pattern with no existing annotation and generate hypotheses or questions people would not otherwise have considered.
